zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check aid: [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The supplied page subset was consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription and review notes here are this reviewer’s work, not a reproduction of that dataset. Native scans: Source gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France.

lines.note: The initial rimo completes Itçuyo from the preceding page, giving a statement that the speaker feels worse than ever. Qibun axǔ gozaru is matched by the Portuguese continuation below; keep particu / larmente divided without inventing a hyphen.

runs.text: larmente mais que ſempre meacho mal.

lines.note: This completes particularmente and the translation that the speaker now feels especially unwell. Preserve the printed joined meacho rather than separating it to modern me acho.
Itçumade asks until when. The short Portuguese gloss ends with a period, not a question mark; retain the draft grave on Atè where the small mark is not clearly contrary.

The head names a plant, with the poetry label P. and a Japanese explanation meaning grass growing on walls. Keep the caron on xǒzuru and the long s in cuſa. Separate second-pass enlargement shows the P’s sloping stem and italic foot; the full label is italic rather than the draft’s split P/period styling.

runs.text: Erua aßi chamada que nace nas paredes, &

lines.note: The Portuguese identifies a so-called herb growing on walls. Erua, nace, and the ß of aßi agree with the historical wording; the line does not identify a modern botanical species.

runs.text: logo ſe ſeca: tomaſe por breue tempo, ou couſa

lines.note: The plant quickly dries and serves as a figure for a brief time or a transient thing. Two vertically separated points after ſeca support a colon rather than the draft comma; keep tomaſe joined as printed.
This completes the figurative gloss with perishable and fleeting. The printed perecedeira is retained rather than being modernized, and the short row remains an indented continuation.
The adverb means forever. The grammatical label belongs to the italic apparatus, while the head remains roman; preserve historical Pera.
Itçumo means always. Restore the capital I visible in the scan instead of the draft lowercase initial; the brief gloss is otherwise unchanged.
The repeated expression means always or continually. The scan joins the repeated elements into one headword, which is preserved rather than separated into modern words.
The attributive interrogative is illustrated with itçuno yo, asking which age or era. Preserve the printed yo and the Portuguese question mark; Vt, is italic between the roman forms.
A second example asks at what time. Jibunni belongs to the roman Japanese phrase, and the Portuguese ends with a period even though the phrase is interrogative.
The compound verb concerns cherishing or lavishing attention and favors. Preserve the printed space within the head phrase, the principal parts u, uita, and the physical a- / gaſalhados division.
This completes the Portuguese account of many attentions and favors. The historical fauores and the initial fragment of agaſalhados remain exactly at this physical line.

The phrase indicates uncertainty about the time. Preserve the dictionary’s wording Não ſei tè quando and the caron on nǒ; the example ends with a visible hyphen, with no independent period after it as suggested by the draft.

runs.text: Estou doente não ſei tè quãdo.

lines.note: This completes Itçuto-nǒ vazzurǒ, an example of illness with uncertain duration. The two long-o carons and the nasal abbreviation in quãdo are visible and are retained without modernization.
The adverb means at any time. Preserve the nasal abbreviation tẽpo and the italic Adu. and Vt, before the Japanese example below.

The example says the speaker will never forget the addressee’s favors. Keep gôvonuo with the draft circumflex where the worn small mark supplies no positive contrary reading; vaſuremai has long s, and Nun- continues into nunca.

runs.text: ca jamais me eſquecerei de voßos beneficios.

lines.note: This completes the promise never to forget the addressee’s benefits. The long s in eſquecerei and the ß of voßos are retained; no accent is supplied to beneficios.
Itçuuari is a lie or pretense. The Portuguese clearly supports fingimento rather than draft fungimento; the paragraph begins an example whose noun is divided Itçu- / uariuo.
The example literally concerns saying a falsehood and is glossed to lie or pretend. The meaning and visible f cross-stroke support fingir, not draft ſingir; the caron on yǔ is retained.
The corresponding verb repeats the meanings to lie or pretend. The printed headword and its u, atta principal parts are kept, rather than expanded into modern conjugated forms.
The scan shows u after ç, supporting Itçuxica rather than draft Itçixica. The gloss asks at what hour or time, with a visible question mark; the final S. is a separate roman written-usage label.
The entry means not knowing when. The first Portuguese word is Não, with a rounded final o rather than OCR r; the example repeats the roman Japanese head at the end of this line.

The Japanese asks what has become of the matter discussed at some unspecified earlier time. The visible cauaita is retained without inserting an expected consonant; the caron on mǒxi and the question mark are supported by the scan.

runs.text: falamos não ſei oraquando, como vai?

lines.note: The translation asks how the previously discussed matter is going. Preserve the locally aligned joined oraquando, whose internal spacing is not decisively wider than ordinary letter spacing, and the final question mark.
Itçuzo is presented here as at some time. The example begins with the honorific võ before meni on the next row; keep its tilde rather than expanding the nasal abbreviation.

The example concerns meeting and speaking to someone. Enlargement shows a short s, with two surviving curved portions, in mǒsǒzu rather than draft mǒtǒzu; both carons are visible. The Portuguese word is hora, not bora, and the tilde in algũa remains over u.
This completes the translation that the speaker will meet him and speak to him. The historical double l in elle is clear; this line is wholly Portuguese and remains italic.

A separate entry groups the alternatives itçuzo and itçuzoya with the meaning not knowing when. The printed lowercase l introduces an alternative, and the question mark is retained even after the declarative Portuguese wording.
The verb refers to a damp substance freezing or hardening in the cold. Retain the source spelling Enregelarſe and the divided co- / mo rather than modernizing the Portuguese.

runs.text: mo parede de barro freſca, &c. & fazerſe

lines.note: The gloss gives a fresh earthen wall as an example and continues with becoming hard. Both ampersands and the repeated connective structure are printed and are preserved.
This completes the freezing entry: becoming hard with cold. The short line is wholly italic Portuguese and remains attached by indentation to the preceding definition.
This separate ite means an archer. The two Japanese descriptions of an accomplished archer are linked by l; retain Iǒzuno with consonantal I and the printed cuqiǒ, not a modernized romanization.

runs.text: Destro em tirar com arco. Aliquã

lines.note: The second Japanese phrase is completed, then glossed as skillful in shooting a bow. Aliquã continues into do on the next line; its abbreviation and lack of a clear terminal hyphen are retained.

runs.text: do, O que tira com eſpingarda.

lines.note: The occasional additional sense is someone who shoots a firearm. Preserve the capital O following the divided Aliquã-do and the historical eſpingarda spelling.

Itei is explained by the Japanese phrase a different or unusual form, followed by a gloss of an exceptionally ugly or lowly appearance. Keep the Japanese explanation roman and the physical extra / ordinariamente division unjoined.

This completes extraordinariamente and specifies appearance and clothing. The italic example marker follows the Portuguese gloss; retain the locally aligned short s in vestidos rather than standardizing all st sequences.
The Japanese example concedes that the speaker’s appearance is unattractive or lowly. The whole quotation, including its &c., is in roman type; naricoſo retains its visible long s.

The roman Monog. is a citation label before the translation, not part of the Japanese example or the Portuguese sentence. The translation begins although my appearance and manner; retain poſto and the draft short s in gesto.

This completes the concessive translation and begins a new example using the adjectival form iteina. Preserve the printed separate toda via and the switch back to roman Japanese after the paragraph mark.

runs.text: Figura, ou vulto de peßoa magra,

lines.note: The Japanese phrase concerns an unattractive appearance. Its Portuguese explanation specifies the figure or face of a thin person; catachi is a continuation, not an independent headword.
The gloss further describes the person as wasted and lowly in appearance. Preserve the source’s short s in desfeita and the independent indented physical row.

runs.text: Aldea, ou reino fora da Chi

lines.note: The head is Iteqi: the narrow t is visibly present after I and was lost in the draft. The Japanese gloss Inaca and the Portuguese description of a village or realm outside China are preserved literally; Chi continues on the next row.

This completes China and gives iteqino fito, people characterized by the dictionary as barbarians or foreigners. The repetition of Iteqi confirms the headword reading above; the historical characterization is the source’s wording, not an editorial classification.
This completes eſtrã-geiros and specifies people from outside China. The physical split and the source’s geographical frame are retained without updating the terminology.

The Japanese gloss means good people, matched by Bom pouo. The head begins Itmin, not OCR Ftmin: the margin rule crosses the capital I and creates a false crossbar. The worn o in Yoi is retained from the visible lower curve and the coherent Japanese gloss.

Itmot is followed by the Japanese explanatory phrase Foxij mamano mono and then a Portuguese gloss continued below. Preserve the abbreviated final -t and the source’s wording even though the two glosses are not a simple literal match. The mark after i has a descending tail, supporting i, rather than i.

runs.text: ca, ou excellente, como falcão, caualo, & cão.

lines.note: This completes vni-ca: a unique or excellent specimen, such as a falcon, horse, or dog. The crossed x is visible in excellente, correcting OCR eecellente; preserve the historical caualo.
This ito is thread or a strand. The brief head and two synonymous Portuguese nouns agree with the scan and are distinct from the homographic adverb below.

runs.text: Adu. Com razão, ou muito. Vt,

lines.note: The adverb is glossed as with reason or very. Keep both source senses and the italic grammatical apparatus; the roman Ito at the end begins its example.
The example says that something is very easy. Preserve the joined cotonari and the long s in yaſui; no modern accents are supplied to He or facil.
Itoco means cousin. The Portuguese gloss is kinship terminology here rather than a statement of rank or quality, and the source leaves it as a one-word definition.
Itocodoxi is referred to the preceding cousin entry with Idem. The final xi spelling is visible and is not replaced with modern dōshi spelling or a supplied long-vowel mark.

runs.text: Proueitos, & bẽs que nacem de hum ter

lines.note: The head concerns benefits or advantages arising from a person’s power and prosperity. Keep the nasal abbreviation bẽs and historical nacem; the construction hum ter continues into the next row.
This completes the explanation of benefits arising from power and worldly splendor or prosperity. Preserve the locally aligned short s in fausto despite the joined st letterforms.
The adverb is glossed as much or deeply. The colon introduces a further usage explanation on the following rows; it is not changed to a period.

runs.text: ordinaria mente ſe vſa em comparação de outra

lines.note: The usage note says the adverb is normally used in comparison with something else. The visible letters support comparação rather than draft compiração; retain the draft separation ordinaria mente where the worn spacing is not decisive.
The compared thing is contrary or opposed. Preserve the printed contraposta with the locally aligned short s, and keep the italic Vt, before the verse example.

The first verse line expresses intensified longing for what is past. The visible ſuguinixi and coixiqini form coherent historical Japanese; this is an entire roman example line, not Japanese words embedded in Portuguese.

The second verse line envies the waves that can return. The scan ends with a tall stroke above a separate dot, supporting an exclamation mark rather than the draft period; retain the initial V and the cayeru spelling.

runs.text: Tẽdo grãdes ſaudades do Miyaco, & do q̃ dei

lines.note: The Portuguese paraphrase describes great longing for Miyaco and what has been left behind. Miyaco is a Japanese name embedded in the Portuguese sentence; retain all visible nasal abbreviations and the physical dei / xo division.

runs.text: xo a tras, vẽdo eſtas ondas q̃ chegão à praya,

lines.note: This completes deixo and describes watching waves reach the shore. Preserve separate a tras, historical praya, and the vowel carriers of vẽdo and chegão rather than expanding or normalizing them.

runs.text: & ſe tornão, ò que ſaudades, & magoa terei

lines.note: The paraphrase contrasts the waves returning with the speaker’s longing and sorrow. The exclamatory ò carries the printed grave; no modern accent is supplied to magoa.
This ends the verse paraphrase: the speaker cannot return. Preserve the ß in poßo and the final period; the line is not a new dictionary entry.

runs.text: Fios com que estão coſidas, ou pega-

lines.note: Itogue denotes the cords used to sew or fasten armor pieces together. The conjunction is ou rather than draft os, supported by the u-shaped strokes and the two coordinated participles; retain pega- as the physical division.

runs.text: das as peças das armas hũas com outras.

lines.note: This completes pegadas and explains that the armor pieces are attached to one another. The nasal abbreviation in hũas is retained without expansion, and the whole continuation remains italic.

runs.text: Deixar, ou dar de mão. Vt,

lines.note: The verb is glossed as leaving or renouncing. Both long-o marks are visibly circumflexes; retain ô, ôta rather than converting them to carons from a different entry.

The example means renouncing the world and entering religious life. The round vowel after Y supports Youo, not the draft Ybuo; xucqe retains the dictionary’s consonant notation for becoming a religious renunciant.

The translation completes renouncing the world and becoming a religious person; mundo corrects OCR mindo. A new example then introduces rejection or contempt of oneself, with the printed circumflex on itô.
After the gloss to despise oneself, another example concerns aversion to the wind. The scan supports Cajeuo with j and itô with a circumflex; these are preserved rather than modernized.

runs.text: Sentir, & moſtrar repugnancia ao vento Vt,

lines.note: The gloss explains feeling and displaying aversion to the wind. The source runs directly into Vt, without a securely visible intervening period; do not add one from expected punctuation.

runs.text: Miſuuo fuqicayeſu cajeuo ſaye fitoyato ito

lines.note: The example describes wind lifting or blowing back a screen, with apprehension that it might be a person. The visible open c after fuqi supports fuqicayeſu rather than draft fuqieayeſu. Keep the long s in Miſuuo, cayeſu, and ſaye and the line-end fragment ito.

This completes the printed verb beginning ito on the preceding row. Retain uaxeraretani as printed rather than replacing its historical ending; the Portuguese starts a conditional comparison about aversion to the wind.

runs.text: vento que entraua polla janella, & aleuanta-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes wind entering through the window and lifting something. Preserve historical polla, janella, and the physical division aleuanta- / ua.

runs.text: ua as eſteiras duuidando ſe era homem que as

lines.note: This completes aleuantaua and explains the uncertainty whether a person was lifting the screens or mats. The source’s eſteiras and duuidando remain literal, with their long s and u/v spellings.
The comparison concludes with how much more, and a new example begins with Cata-, continued as qi below. The paragraph belongs to the same itoi entry; no new headword is created.

runs.text: qino tameni inochiuo vxinauã cotouo ito

lines.note: The Japanese example concerns losing one’s life on account of an enemy. The printed tilde is on the final a of vxinauã, and the verb is again physically divided ito / uazu.
The Japanese negative itouazu is glossed as not shrinking from or fearing the loss of life. Preserve the Portuguese double r in arreceaua and the per- / der division.

runs.text: der a vida pera com os inimigos.

lines.note: This completes perder a vida and explains risking life against enemies. A visible space separates der and a, correcting draft dera; the upright i, is kept outside the italic explanation it introduces. Retain the nasal abbreviation and division ẽ- / contrar.
This completes encontrar and the clarification about facing the enemies. The double l in elles is printed, and the short line remains an indented Portuguese continuation.
Itoma is leave or permission. The first construction concerns granting leave and offers an alternative verb below; the final mark after l visibly descends as a comma rather than the draft period.
Yaru completes the alternatives for granting leave. A new construction concerns requesting it; the mark on cô is a circumflex, distinct from the caron in the next verb.
The alternative mǒſu completes asking for leave, then the next construction begins with ta-. Keep its caron and long s and the visible ta- / mauaru division.

runs.text: Auer, ou receber licença do ſe-

lines.note: This completes tamauaru and explains receiving leave from a superior. Preserve historical Auer and the divided ſe- / nhor rather than modernizing either the spelling or lineation.
The short row completes ſenhor and the leave-granting explanation. Its full text and final period fit within the inspected crop, and it is retained as its own indented row.
Itomagoi denotes leave-taking or a farewell. The source head and Portuguese noun agree; no additional gloss or usage label is printed.
The verb means killing by shooting with a bow or firearm. Preserve the three-part head and the printed eſpin- / garda division; the following line supplies the animal or bird as object.
This completes eſpingarda and specifies killing an animal or bird. The apparently loose comma after garda and the ß in paßaro are source features, not editorial corrections.
Itonami concerns business, activity, or management. Retain the historical nouns feitura and meneo rather than substituting modern near-synonyms; the entry introduces several examples below.
The first example concerns worldly livelihood. The caron on Tǒxeino is faint but compatible with the retained draft reading; the Portuguese tra- is visibly divided before to on the next row.

runs.text: to do mundo pera paſſar a vida. ¶

lines.note: This completes the explanation of worldly affairs for making a living, then begins an example concerning the afterlife. Preserve the printed double long s in paſſar and the caron plus hyphen in Goxǒ-.

The Japanese example concerns attending to one’s afterlife; the Portuguese interprets it as working for salvation. Preserve the visible long s and the tilde on the final a of ſaluação without a supplied final period.

The final example concerns managing a household. Its Portuguese translation begins Nego and continues onto the next page; the separate ciar, below is a catchword, not a second body continuation to be merged here.
